title: AI Investors Hedge Losses as Tech Stocks Plunge: Jerusalem Post Reports Market Shift
body:
Investors who rode the AI boom wave are now scrambling for insurance as the sector’s once‑soaring stocks slump and financing costs climb. Hedge funds, family offices and even retail traders have turned to a mix of put options, credit‑default swaps and other derivatives to lock in gains and cap exposure, signaling a sharp shift from exuberant betting to defensive positioning.

The rally that propelled AI‑related equities to multi‑year highs began in early 2023, when venture capital and public‑market money poured into firms promising to embed machine‑learning algorithms into everything from cloud services to autonomous vehicles. Companies such as Nvidia, Microsoft, and a host of niche AI chip makers saw market capitalisations swell, while dozens of start‑ups secured multi‑billion‑dollar valuations on the back of hype about “generative AI” breakthroughs. Yet, as the initial euphoria faded, a confluence of factors has begun to erode that optimism. Rising interest rates have made borrowing more expensive for high‑growth firms that rely on leverage, while earnings reports from several marquee names have missed consensus forecasts, prompting analysts to downgrade price targets. The result: a broad‑based correction that has knocked more than 30 % off the AI index since its peak in November.

In response, market participants are employing a layered risk‑management strategy. The most visible move is the surge in purchase of out‑of‑the‑money put options on AI‑heavy ETFs and on individual stocks such as Nvidia and AMD. According to data from the Options Clearing Corporation, the open interest in AI‑related puts has more than doubled in the past six weeks, reflecting a growing appetite for downside protection. Simultaneously, credit‑default swap (CDS) spreads on several AI‑focused corporate bonds have widened, indicating that investors are pricing in a higher probability of default should the sector’s cash flows deteriorate further. Some hedge funds are also constructing “collar” positions—simultaneously buying puts and selling calls—to lock in a price range while still collecting premium income.

The defensive shift is not limited to large institutions. Retail investors, many of whom entered the market through commission‑free platforms, are now using “protective puts” and “stop‑loss orders” to guard modest portfolios that had benefitted from the AI rally. Financial advisors warn that the allure of high‑growth AI stocks can mask underlying volatility, especially as macro‑economic headwinds—such as tighter monetary policy and a slowing global growth outlook—loom large. “We’re seeing a classic case of investors recalibrating after a period of speculative excess,” said Maya Patel, a senior analyst at Global Equity Research. “The tools they’re using now are standard hedging instruments, but the speed at which they’re being deployed suggests a heightened sense of urgency.”

While the current defensive posture may temper short‑term price swings, it also hints at a more nuanced market narrative. The AI sector is unlikely to collapse entirely; the underlying technologies continue to attract corporate spend and governmental interest. However, the market is now differentiating between companies with solid fundamentals—steady revenue streams, diversified customer bases, and clear paths to profitability—and those whose valuations were largely built on hype. Firms that can demonstrate sustainable cash flow and a realistic roadmap for product roll‑outs are expected to retain investor confidence, even as broader sentiment cools.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of AI‑related equities will likely be shaped by two interlocking forces: the pace of regulatory developments and the ability of companies to translate laboratory breakthroughs into commercial revenue. If policymakers introduce clearer frameworks for data privacy, model transparency and AI safety, the sector could regain momentum, encouraging investors to unwind some of the protective positions they have stacked. Conversely, if earnings disappointments persist and financing remains costly, the hedging activity may intensify, keeping volatility elevated. For now, the market’s defensive shift serves as a reminder that even the most promising technological revolutions are subject to the same risk‑return calculus that governs every corner of the financial world.
